description:
Who We Are 
We are a team of three university students united by a shared passion for space exploration and creative problem-solving. Our curiosity about the cosmos and human history brings us together to build something meaningful.

Our Interests & Skills 

Our team thrives at the intersection of science, technology, and storytelling. We combine strong skills in software development, data analysis, creative writing, research.
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive web experience that tells the untold stories of NASA’s discarded robotic explorers and equipment on the Moon and Mars. Space agencies know these spacecraft well, yet rarely introduce them to curious school-age learners. We aimed to close that gap by turning complex historical and scientific data into engaging storytelling.

We built a single shareable HTML file with two linked worlds. On the Moon, users tap the remains of Apollo 11’s Eagle lunar module and zoom into a curved timeline: its identity, mission, discoveries (including the EASEP science station), sacrifice, and legacy, illustrated with archival photographs. On Mars, they explore InSight, Phoenix, Spirit, and Opportunity: what they achieved, why they were left behind, and what they made possible later, from dust-repelling panels to using Martian ice for water and fuel.

Each information have imagery or animation with short, story-driven text, turning facts into an emotional journey. Learners form a personal bond with these forgotten explorers and are inspired by their science. It matters because these machines are not scrap metal: they are the foundation of tomorrow’s exploration.
details:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten brings NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars to life through interactive storytelling and a playable game. Spacecraft like Apollo 11’s Eagle lunar module and the Mars landers and rovers are well known to space agencies, but what happened to them after their missions ended is rarely told to children. Our aim is to spark a love of science by sharing this hidden history in language that works for both children and adults.

What we built. A web experience with two connected worlds. On the Moon, players tap the glowing remains of Eagle’s descent stage, the Moon zooms into a half-dome view, and a curved timeline unfolds with five stops: Eagle’s identity, its mission to Mare Tranquillitatis, the discoveries of the EASEP science station, its sacrifice and farewell, and its legacy. On Mars, the remains of InSight, Phoenix, and Spirit & Opportunity each open five chapters about their goals, discoveries, why they were left behind, and the knowledge and technologies they made possible. Archival photographs and animated scenes sit next to short, story-driven text. In the story view, arrow keys (or a swipe on touch screens) move between chapters.

The game. Players move with the W, A, S, and D keys. Pressing Esc lets them switch between the Moon and Mars or return to the presentation. The games purpose is to capture children’s attention and make our stories stick by letting them simulate what we narrate, instead of only reading about it.

Our vision. Exploration doesn’t end when a mission does. We see abandoned spacecraft as silent monuments to human curiosity and as teachers for future scientists and engineers. We want learners to form a personal bond with these forgotten robotic explorers and feel inspired by their science.

How we built it. All the ideas, the concept, and the creative direction came from our team. To bring them to life, we built the entire experience, including the game, with AI, using Claude and Gemini. We also created the translations with these tools, and our team reviewed and checked them.

Why it matters. Every explorer left on the Moon and Mars carries lessons for tomorrow’s missions. By telling their stories in an accessible, emotional way, we help young people discover science and help adults rediscover it.

Who is your story for?

Our story speaks to all age groups, but we primarily targeted school-age young people who are curious about space.

How accessible is your chosen format?

Very accessible. We used simple, clear language that anyone can understand, and the experience runs in a web browser as a single shareable file, so no special software is needed.

Specific missions and equipment, or a broader story?

We followed the sources and information provided to us and focused on specific missions and equipment: Apollo 11’s Eagle and the EASEP science station on the Moon, and InSight, Phoenix, Spirit, and Opportunity on Mars. Through them, we informed players about NASA’s wider story of exploration.

Which perspectives do you want to highlight?

We highlight how these discarded explorers shape todays and tomorrows space technologies, from the knowledge they gathered to the ideas their missions inspired.
